---
title: "Ethics, liability, and the device boundary: who answers for the note"
subtitle: "AIM-4 · AIM-7 · AIM-X · about 75 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. State that no US malpractice claim involving a clinical AI tool has reached
   a verdict, and describe what a plaintiff would have to prove anyway.
2. Place a clinical scenario in the Price, Gerke, and Cohen 2×2 and say which
   cell carries the most exposure and why.
3. Describe the Jabbour finding, including the part where explanations did not
   help, and say what it implies about "explainable AI" as a safety control.
4. State FDA's four criteria for non-device clinical decision support and
   explain why the fourth decides most real cases.
5. Explain what a Predetermined Change Control Plan is and why it is the
   mechanism that makes a model that keeps changing regulable at all.
6. Say what to document, whom to tell, and what contract to ask about when an
   AI tool touches a note, and find the current primary-source answer to a
   regulatory question that has moved since this chapter was written.
7. Write down one part of clinical judgment you will not delegate, and what
   would have to be true for you to change your mind.
:::

**Time.** About 25 minutes of reading, 20 minutes of listening, 25 minutes of
doing, and five minutes of writing at the end that are the point of the whole
course. You need a browser and nothing else. No chatbot is required; where one
helps, your institutional ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account is enough. Nothing
installs, and nothing in this chapter touches a real patient's data.

## The sentence you did not write

It is the third month of intern year. Your clinic uses an ambient scribe: a
phone app that listens to the visit and drafts the note. Mr. Alvarez, 68, has
atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban. Halfway through the visit he mentions,
almost in passing, that he stopped it two weeks ago because of nosebleeds, and
you talk about that for a minute before moving on to his knee. The scribe's
draft is waiting when you get back to the workroom. It is 6:40 in the evening,
you have fourteen notes to sign, and this one reads well.

::: {.ehr-note}
<div class="hdr"><span>Progress note · Internal Medicine Clinic</span><span>Signed 18:47 · Intern (PGY-1)</span></div>
<div class="sec">Subjective</div>
<p>68M with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc 4), HTN, and right knee OA presents for follow-up. <mark>Continues apixaban 5 mg BID without bleeding complications.</mark> Reports 3 weeks of right knee pain, worse with stairs, no trauma. Denies chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations.</p>
<div class="sec">Assessment and plan</div>
<p>AF, rate controlled: continue apixaban and metoprolol.<br>Right knee OA: trial of acetaminophen; PT referral; RTC 8 weeks.</p>
<div class="foot">Draft generated by ambient documentation. Reviewed and signed by the clinician. <em>Illustrative note for this chapter; synthetic patient; not any vendor's or institution's material.</em></div>

:::

Read the highlighted sentence. It is the kind of error the published studies
of these tools describe: not a transcription slip, but a fluent, plausible
sentence that is the opposite of what the patient said. In a pilot at one
academic system, physicians reviewed 356 scribe-drafted notes; 18% contained an
omission, 11.5% contained a fabricated statement, and 5.3% contained an error
rated as posing serious risk if not corrected, while 14.9% of all notes were
signed with no edits at all [@pmid:41996389].

Three weeks later Mr. Alvarez is admitted with a stroke. The admitting team
reads your note. Then the hospital's risk manager reads it, and asks you a
question that has one answer: *who wrote this sentence?* The note has your
name on it. The waiting room has a sign about "AI-assisted documentation" and
the medical assistant mentions it at check-in; whether that is consent is, as
you will see, a question being litigated right now.

Nobody in this scenario has done anything unusual. That is the problem this
chapter is about: what the law, the regulator, and your own judgment have to
say when a tool that is allowed to be in the room is wrong, and your name is
on the result.

## Why this matters

You will sign a note drafted by software within a year of starting residency,
possibly within a week. You will silence a prediction alert, follow a
recommendation you cannot fully explain, and override one you can. Each of
those is a decision that a lawyer, a regulator, and a patient could later ask
you to account for. The rules for doing so are partly written, partly moving,
and partly not written at all.

The honest version of the law is short. **No US malpractice claim involving a
clinical AI tool has reached a verdict as of the date on this chapter.** The
students who arrive expecting a rule to memorize leave with something more
durable: a framework for reasoning about exposure, one regulatory boundary you
can actually learn, one hard experimental finding about what a bad model does
to the clinicians who trust it, and a written position of your own. That last
item is the reason this chapter closes the course.

## The idea

### No court has answered yet, and what a plaintiff must prove anyway

Malpractice is a species of negligence, and negligence has four elements. The
plaintiff must show that you owed the patient a duty (you did; he was your
patient), that you breached the **standard of care**, meaning what a
reasonably competent physician in your position would have done, that the
breach caused the harm, and that the harm was real. The tool is not a
defendant in that sentence. It is evidence. Current doctrine measures the
*physician* against the standard-of-care benchmark, not the AI against
anything [@pmid:31584609; @pmid:38231630].

Two consequences follow. First, "the AI was wrong" is not, by itself, a legal
theory. The question a court will ask is whether *you* should have known
better than to rely on the output, given what you had in front of you
[@pmid:38231630]. Second, suing the vendor instead is harder than it sounds.
Courts have historically treated clinical software as a service rather than a
product, and the **learned intermediary doctrine**, the rule that a
manufacturer's duty to warn runs to the physician who stands between the
product and the patient, places the treating clinician's judgment in the
middle of the chain. Price, Gerke, and Cohen note that this may shift as tools
become opaque enough that physician scrutiny is no longer realistic, but it is
where the law stands today
([Price, Gerke, and Cohen, 2024](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613216/)).

Mr. Alvarez's note, then, would not be litigated as "the scribe made an
error." It would be litigated as "the physician signed a note stating the
patient was taking a medication he had told her he had stopped." Whether that
is below the standard of care at 6:40 p.m. with fourteen notes to sign is
exactly the question no court has yet answered.

::: {.callout-note title="Your insurer, briefly"}
Malpractice carriers have not written AI out of their policies. The Doctors
Company has said publicly that it has no AI exclusion and would defend and
indemnify a physician when AI played a role in a claim; the broader market
pattern is case-by-case underwriting and advice to tell your carrier before
adopting a clinical AI tool
[VERIFY: statement reported in Medical Economics, 2025; confirm against the carrier's own policy language](https://www.medicaleconomics.com/view/ai-on-trial-how-malpractice-insurers-can-help-physicians-navigate-new-risks){.verify}.
For a resident, the coverage that matters first is your institution's, and
someone in the GME office can tell you what it says. Ask in orientation, not
after.
:::

### Four cells

Price, Gerke, and Cohen published the framework that everyone since has used
[@pmid:31584609]. Two questions define it: did the AI's recommendation match
the standard of care, and did the physician follow it? That gives four cells.

| | **Physician followed the AI** | **Physician overrode the AI** |
|---|---|---|
| **AI matched the standard of care** | A. Good outcome likely; if harm occurs, exposure is low. Can following a correct recommendation you could not explain still create exposure? | C. High exposure. The physician departed from the standard of care *and* disagreed with a tool that got it right. |
| **AI departed from the standard of care** | B. High exposure. The physician did the nonstandard thing because the machine said so. | D. The physician was right. Residual exposure lives in documentation, institutional policy, and the fact that the tool stayed deployed. |

: The Price, Gerke, and Cohen 2×2. Rows are what the AI said; columns are what the physician did. {#tbl-price}

The uncomfortable cell is B. Under current doctrine, the physician who
*follows* the AI into nonstandard care carries the most risk, which
structurally discourages using AI precisely where it would most change
management [@pmid:31584609]. The other high-exposure cell is C, and it raises a
different worry: once a tool is in the room, does a clinician have to justify
*disagreeing* with it?

Two experiments have asked potential jurors. In a nationally representative
sample of 2,000 US adults, physicians who followed an AI recommendation for
standard care were judged less liable than those who rejected it, while
rejecting a *nonstandard* recommendation provided no similar shield
[@pmid:32978285]. A 2026 replication across US and German adults and German
physicians, the people who would sit as lay jurors in one system and
court-appointed experts in the other, found the same pattern: accepting
standard-care AI advice was rated more reasonable than rejecting it, and
accepting or rejecting nonstandard advice was judged about the same
[@pmid:42242875]. Read against @tbl-price, the practical lesson is that the
tool is safest to follow when it agrees with what you would have done anyway,
and that the moment it disagrees, you are on your own in either direction.

Where does Mr. Alvarez's note sit? Nowhere on the grid, at first glance: the
scribe made no recommendation. But the note *is* a recommendation once
signed. "Continue apixaban" was the plan, written on a premise the patient had
contradicted, and you followed it. Cell B, by a side door.

### Explanations did not help

The reflexive institutional answer to all of this is "we will require
explainable AI." That answer has been tested once, in a randomized study, and
in that test it did not work.

Jabbour and colleagues gave 457 hospitalists, nurse practitioners, and
physician assistants clinical vignettes of acute respiratory failure and asked
them to judge the likelihood of pneumonia, heart failure, and COPD. Baseline
accuracy was 73.0%. A standard AI model raised accuracy by 2.9 points, or 4.4
points when the model also showed its reasoning as an image-based explanation.
A *systematically biased* model lowered accuracy by 11.3 points. Adding
explanations to the biased model recovered 2.3 points, a difference whose
confidence interval crossed zero [@pmid:38112814].

![The Jabbour finding, redrawn from the paper's own numbers. Explanations
helped a little when the model was right and did not significantly help when
the model was wrong. Data from Jabbour et al., *JAMA* 2023;330:2275–2284;
figure drawn for this chapter.](../images/jabbour-2023-explanations.svg){#fig-jabbour fig-alt="Bar chart of change in clinician diagnostic accuracy in percentage points from a 73.0% baseline. Standard AI model without explanation plus 2.9; with explanation plus 4.4; biased model without explanation minus 11.3; biased model with explanation minus 9.1. Whiskers show 95% confidence intervals; the two biased-model intervals overlap."}

Hold that against @tbl-price. A defense built on "the tool showed its
reasoning, so the physician should have caught it" has to contend with
evidence that showing the reasoning did not help the clinicians who were
shown it. And a plaintiff in cell B has the same paper: the physician was
handed a biased model, and the safeguard everyone relies on was shown not to
work. **Automation bias**, the tendency to over-rely on a suggestion from an
automated system, is not fixed by adding a paragraph of rationale. It is a
property of tired humans under time pressure, which is what you will be.

### The device boundary

Software that gives clinicians recommendations is either a medical device,
regulated by FDA, or it is not. The line is drawn by four criteria in the
statute (section 520(o)(1)(E) of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act), and FDA's
guidance on how it reads them is the single regulatory document worth knowing
by heart. Software is **non-device clinical decision support** only if it
meets all four:

1. It is **not** intended to acquire, process, or analyze a medical image, or
   a signal from an in vitro diagnostic or a signal-acquisition system.
2. It is intended to display, analyze, or print medical information.
3. It is intended to *support or provide recommendations* to a health care
   professional about prevention, diagnosis, or treatment.
4. It is intended to enable that professional to **independently review the
   basis** for the recommendation, so that they do not rely primarily on it
   to make the decision for an individual patient.

Criterion 4 decides most real cases. A bare risk score with no visible
rationale fails it. The same score with its inputs, its logic, and the
validation behind it displayed, in plain language, may pass. In the current
guidance FDA says outright that it does not consider software intended for a
time-critical decision to meet criterion 4, because the clinician will not have
time to review the basis, and it names automation bias as the reason
([FDA, Clinical Decision Support Software, guidance issued January 29, 2026](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/clinical-decision-support-software)).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-cds-path
%%| fig-cap: "The four criteria as a path. Any 'no' makes the software a device. Criterion 4 is where most real tools are decided, and it is a question about what the clinician can see, not about how accurate the model is."
flowchart TD
  q1{"Does it analyze an image,<br/>an IVD signal, or a signal<br/>from a monitor?"} -- yes --> dev[Device: FDA oversight]
  q1 -- no --> q2{"Does it display or analyze<br/>medical information?"}
  q2 -- no --> dev
  q2 -- yes --> q3{"Does it support or provide<br/>recommendations to a clinician?"}
  q3 -- "no (directs the decision,<br/>or is patient-facing)" --> dev
  q3 -- yes --> q4{"Can the clinician independently<br/>review the basis, with time to do so?"}
  q4 -- "no (black box,<br/>or time-critical)" --> dev
  q4 -- yes --> nd[Non-device CDS:<br/>no FDA review]
```

A sepsis alert that fires from vital-sign trends and tells the nurse to page
you is a device on criterion 1 (it processes monitor signals) and probably on
criterion 4 (it is time-critical). A tool that matches a patient's diagnosis
to a guideline and shows you the guideline is non-device CDS. A large language
model that answers a clinical question in fluent prose with no visible source
is a harder case than either, and FDA has not yet said where it falls: the
agency published a discussion paper on generative-AI-enabled devices in August
2026 that names hallucination as the property that distinguishes these tools
and asks for comment by 19 October 2026, but a discussion paper is not
guidance
([FDA, *Considerations for the Regulation of Generative AI-Enabled Medical Devices*, August 18, 2026](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/digital-health-center-excellence/considerations-regulation-generative-ai-enabled-medical-devices-discussion-paper-and-request)).
Your scribe, notably, is not a device at all under any of this. It makes no
recommendation. It writes what it heard, or what it thinks it heard, and the
regulator that reviews it is you.

::: {.callout-important title="This boundary moved twice while the course was being written"}
The four criteria come from a 2016 statute. FDA's guidance on them was issued
in September 2022, replaced on January 6, 2026, and replaced again on
January 29, 2026, which is the version linked above. The January revisions
were framed as deregulatory; the main substantive change is that FDA will now
tolerate a tool that gives a *single* recommendation where only one is
clinically appropriate, rather than insisting on a list. The four criteria
themselves did not change. Before you rely on anything in this section, open
the FDA page and check the date at the top. That check is the skill; the
content is the example.
:::

### A model that changes

Clearance is granted to a specific version of a specific algorithm. Most
modern models are updated continuously. So what, exactly, is cleared?

FDA's answer, finalized in December 2024, is the **Predetermined Change
Control Plan**, or PCCP. A manufacturer describes, in the original submission,
the modifications it anticipates making, the protocol it will follow to make
and validate them, and an assessment of their impact. Updates that fall inside
the plan do not trigger a new review. This is the mechanism that lets a
learning model ship improvements without going back to FDA each time, and it
is the single most important regulatory concept for a physician who will use
these tools
([FDA, PCCP guidance, final, December 4, 2024](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/marketing-submission-recommendations-predetermined-change-control-plan-artificial-intelligence)).
It also raises the question worth putting to any vendor: if the model on my
unit today is not the model that was cleared, what did clearance tell me?

The critical-appraisal chapter has already made the companion point, and it
belongs here too. Clearance is a regulatory status, not a validation
certificate. Of 130 FDA decision summaries for AI devices, about half reported
clinical performance data and roughly a quarter reported none; among those
with data, well under a third gave sex-specific results [@pmid:33820998]. A
2024 follow-up found the gap persists [@pmid:39187696]. "Cleared" tells you the
manufacturer satisfied FDA that the device is substantially equivalent to
something already on the market. It does not tell you it was tested on
patients like yours.

The one-line teaching irony, if you want it: FDA's own internal
document-review model, Elsa, was rolled out to agency staff in 2025
([FDA press release, December 2025](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-expands-artificial-intelligence-capabilities-agentic-ai-deployment)),
and trade press reported accuracy and hallucination problems in its early
versions [VERIFY: reports of Elsa hallucinations and the Commissioner's acknowledgment; trade press, mid-2025]{.verify}.
The agency writing the rules is working through the same failure modes as
everyone else.

### The note, the patient, and the contract

This is the section the critical-appraisal chapter promised you. Three things
follow when an AI tool touches a note, and they are separate.

**Documentation.** You sign it, you own it. That is not new law; it is the
same rule that applied to a human scribe or a resident's draft. What is new is
the failure mode: a fluent sentence that was never said. Two habits are
defensible in a chart review and cheap at 6:40 p.m. First, read the *plan*
against the *conversation*, not against the draft's own subjective section,
because the draft is internally consistent even when it is wrong. Second,
where your institution's policy calls for it, record that the note was
drafted with ambient documentation and reviewed by you; many systems append
that line automatically, and if yours does, know what it says, because it is
an attestation in your name. The Sharp HealthCare complaint below alleges the
vendor's tool auto-inserted a statement that the patient "consented" to
recording when, the plaintiff says, no one asked. An attestation you did not
write, in a note you signed, is Mr. Alvarez's problem in a different sentence.

**Disclosure.** Whether the patient knows an AI is in the room is an ethical
question first and increasingly a legal one. At one academic center studying
its own ambient-documentation pilot, the most common consent process was a
verbal conversation before the visit; 81.6% of patients consented when given
basic information, falling to 55.3% when told about data storage and corporate
involvement; and when asked who should answer for a documentation error linked
to the tool, 64.1% of patients said the physician [@pmid:40694347]. Those
patients have already decided who wrote the sentence.

::: {.press-clips}
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">KPBS · news</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.kpbs.org/news/health/2025/12/11/lawsuit-claims-sharp-healthcare-secretly-recorded-exam-room-conversations-without-patient-consent">Lawsuit claims Sharp HealthCare secretly recorded exam room conversations without patient consent</a><div class="date">11 December 2025</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">TechTarget · Healthtech Security</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.techtarget.com/healthtechsecurity/news/366641717/Sutter-Health-MemorialCare-face-class-action-lawsuit-over-AI-scribe-use">Sutter Health, MemorialCare face class action lawsuit over AI scribe use</a><div class="date">14 April 2026</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">Becker's Hospital Review</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/strategy/ambient-ai-lawsuit-highlights-importance-of-patient-consent/">Ambient AI lawsuit highlights importance of patient consent</a><div class="date">2026</div></div>
:::

These are complaints, not findings; nothing in them has been adjudicated, and
you should hold them as allegations. The claims are under California's
all-party-consent recording law, its medical-confidentiality statute, and the
federal Wiretap Act, and the plaintiffs' argument in the Sutter case is that
HIPAA compliance alone is not a defense to recording without informed consent.
About a dozen states require every party's consent to record a conversation.
Whether a waiting-room sign satisfies that is what the courts are being asked.
The patient-communication chapter covers how to have the conversation; this
chapter's point is that the conversation is the safeguard, not the sign.

**The contract.** HIPAA, the federal privacy law, permits a covered entity such
as your hospital to share protected health information with a vendor only
under a **business associate agreement**, a contract that makes the vendor
legally responsible for protecting the data. An institution-licensed scribe
or an EHR-embedded model runs under one. The consumer chatbot on your phone
does not, and your institutional ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account does not
either unless your institution says so in writing. The month-one boundary
case from the appraisal chapter resolves as a question: *is there a BAA for
this tool, and does the policy say what I may put into it?* If nobody can
answer in a sentence, the answer is no.

::: {.callout-note title="Your right to see inside the EHR's tools: status as of September 2026"}
The appraisal chapter said you have something close to a legal right to
traceability for decision-support tools inside your EHR, and flagged it for
verification. Here is the resolution. The federal HTI-1 rule (2024) requires
certified EHRs to expose "source attributes" for predictive decision-support
tools: what they were trained on, how they were validated, whether fairness
was tested. **It is in force**, and developers began collecting a year of
real-world performance data in January 2026. But in January 2026 the same
office proposed a deregulatory rule, HTI-5, that would remove the "model
card" source-attribute requirements entirely, on the stated ground that
clinicians rarely opened them. The comment period closed on 27 February 2026;
as of this writing HTI-5 has not been finalized
([ASTP/ONC, HTI-5 proposed rule](https://www.healthit.gov/topic/laws-regulation-and-policy/hti-5-proposed-rule-fact-sheet)).
So: the right exists today and may not next year. The scavenger hunt below
asks someone to check.
:::

### Regulation elsewhere, and the direction of travel

The European Union wrote the only comprehensive AI statute in force. Under the
AI Act, software that is already a regulated medical device is automatically
**high-risk**, with obligations for risk management, data governance, human
oversight, and logging layered on top of device certification. The high-risk
obligations were due in August 2026. In July 2026, under a "Digital Omnibus"
amendment, they were deferred: to December 2027 for standalone high-risk
systems and to August 2028 for AI embedded in regulated products, which is
where medical devices sit
([Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; see the Orrick summary, July 2026](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/07/EU-AI-Act-Update-Digital-Omnibus-Finalizes-8-Compliance-Changes)).
The United States, over the same period, rescinded its 2023 executive order on
AI safety, adopted a deregulatory posture across FDA and ONC, and attempted,
so far without a statute, to preempt state AI laws. The contrast to keep: the
EU *delayed* binding oversight under pressure; the US *removed* federal
oversight and is now arguing with its own states about whether they may add
any. Both facts will be out of date within a year. That is not a reason to
skip them; it is the reason the Do block exists.

### What you keep

The last idea is not legal. In four Polish endoscopy centers that adopted
AI polyp detection, the adenoma detection rate of experienced endoscopists
*doing colonoscopy without the AI* fell from 28.4% before exposure to 22.4%
after, an absolute drop of six points [@pmid:40816301]. The tool did not
malfunction. The clinicians changed. Every framework in this course says the
physician must remain "in the loop," and this is the study that shows the loop
can quietly rewire the physician. The centaur-or-cyborg chapter asked you to
write a policy for which tasks you hand over. This chapter asks the harder
version: which skills you will keep practicing without the tool, so that the
day the tool is wrong, you are still the person the standard of care assumes.

## Watch or listen

**Podcast.** *Stanford Legal*, "Exploring AI in Healthcare: Legal, Regulatory,
and Safety Challenges," with Michelle Mello and Neel Guha (November 21, 2024;
48 min). A full transcript is on the episode page.
<https://law.stanford.edu/stanford-legal/exploring-ai-in-healthcare-legal-regulatory-and-safety-challenges/>

Mello and Guha wrote the *NEJM* liability analysis cited above [@pmid:38231630].
Twenty minutes is enough. Listen for three things: the list of who can be sued
when a tool causes harm (the hospital for how it chose and monitored the tool,
the physician for failing to catch the error, the developer for the design),
the point that courts will ask whether the physician *should have known better
than to rely on this output* rather than comparing the AI with an unaided
human, and the pediatric example of a tool used outside the population it was
built for. Then ask which of the three defendants Mr. Alvarez's lawyer would
name first, and why.

**If you would rather read.** The *NEJM* piece itself, or the Price, Gerke,
and Cohen chapter on liability linked above, which is free on the NCBI
Bookshelf. The older *NEJM AI Grand Rounds* archive has no episode centered on
liability as of this writing; if one appears, it belongs here.

## Do

::: {.callout-warning title="No patient information, ever"}
Nothing in this exercise involves a real patient, a real note, or a
classmate's data. Mr. Alvarez is synthetic. If you use a chatbot at all in
Part A, use it to find documents, not to answer the question; the answer must
come from the primary source, with its URL and the date you checked it.
:::

### Part A: the regulatory scavenger hunt (20 minutes)

This chapter has just told you several things that were true on 7 September
2026. The exercise is to find out whether they still are. Pick **two**
questions below, one from each list. For each, find the current answer from
the primary source (the agency, the statute, the court docket, the
organization's own page), and record the URL and the date you checked.

**List 1: answered in this chapter. Has it moved?**

1. What is the issue date on FDA's current Clinical Decision Support Software
   guidance, and do the four criteria still read as listed above?
2. Has ONC finalized HTI-5? If so, does the decision-support "model card"
   requirement still exist?
3. Has FDA issued generative-AI guidance (not a discussion paper) for
   AI-enabled devices?
4. What is the current EU AI Act deadline for high-risk AI embedded in medical
   devices?
5. Has any US malpractice claim involving a clinical AI tool reached a
   verdict? (Search the legal press; if you find one, you have found something
   this chapter's author could not.)

**List 2: open when this chapter was written.**

6. What do ACGME or LCME currently require of residency programs or medical
   schools regarding AI training? Find the standard's own text.
7. What is the status of the National Academy of Medicine's AI Code of
   Conduct, and where is the current version published?
8. Has a patient-facing clinical chatbot safety incident been documented since
   the 2023 National Eating Disorders Association "Tessa" case? Name it and its
   primary source.
9. What has happened in the Sharp HealthCare or Sutter Health ambient-scribe
   cases since April 2026? (Court docket or a law-firm summary, not a vendor
   blog.)
10. Does your own institution have a written policy on ambient documentation,
    on consent for it, and on which AI tools carry a business associate
    agreement? Find the document, or record who told you none exists.

Record it like this; it is your artifact.

```
Question ___ (List 1)
Primary source URL: ______________________________________________
Date checked: ____________   Document date shown on the source: ____________
Has it moved since 2026-09-07?   Y / N / cannot tell
If yes, what changed, in one sentence: ____________________________________
Did two credible sources disagree?  Y / N   If yes, which and how: __________

Question ___ (List 2)
Primary source URL: ______________________________________________
Date checked: ____________
The answer, in one sentence: _______________________________________________
Confidence that this is the *current* answer (1-5): ___   Why: ____________
```

The finding students usually bring back is that several of these have no
clean answer even at the primary source, and that two credible outlets say
different things. That is not a failure of the exercise. It is the honest
state of the field, and being able to say "the primary source is dated X and
says Y, and I could not confirm Z" is a skill you will need in five years,
when everything specific in this chapter has been replaced.

### Part B: your side of the case (10 minutes)

Go back to Mr. Alvarez. Answer in writing:

1. **Which cell of @tbl-price** is the note in, and why? (One sentence. If you
   think it is not on the grid, say what the "recommendation" was.)
2. **What would a plaintiff have to prove**, in the four elements, and which
   element is hardest for them?
3. **The single fact that, if changed, would flip your answer.** This is the
   real artifact. Was it the time of day? The number of notes? Whether the
   attestation line was auto-inserted? Whether the clinic's policy required
   reading the plan against the conversation? Whether Mr. Alvarez knew the
   scribe was running? Name one, and say which way it flips.
4. **Which of the four CDS criteria** would the sepsis alert on your next
   inpatient rotation fail, and does it matter to *you* that it is a device?

You are not asked what a court *would* hold. There is no case law to be right
about. You are asked what a court *should* hold, and why.

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Two scavenger-hunt answers | Each has a primary-source URL, the date you checked, and the date on the source | A secondary summary, or no date |
| The "has it moved" judgment | You can say whether the source is newer than 2026-09-07 and what changed | "Seems the same" |
| A cell for the note | A cell of @tbl-price, with the recommendation named | "It depends" |
| The four elements | Duty, breach, causation, damages, and which is hardest here | "The AI was wrong" |
| The flipping fact | One specific fact and the direction it flips the ruling | A list of everything that matters |
| The device question | Which criterion the alert fails, in your own words | "It's FDA-cleared so it's fine" |
| The Jabbour sentence | You can say what explanations did and did not do, with the direction of the numbers | "Explainable AI helps" |
| The PCCP sentence | You can say what clearance covers when the model has been updated | "It was cleared" |
| Your position | Three sentences below, with a falsifiable condition | A slogan |

## The standing question

This is the closing question of the course, and it is the reason this chapter
is last. Write three sentences. Do not write a slogan.

> **What part of clinical judgment will you not delegate to an AI system, and
> what would have to be true for you to change your mind?**

The second clause does the work. Without it, you will write something that
sounds like a value. With it, you have to state a condition under which you
would be wrong, which converts a reflex into a position you can defend and,
more importantly, revise. Go back to the policy you wrote in the
centaur-or-cyborg chapter and put this sentence at the bottom of it. Then put
Mr. Alvarez at the bottom of that: it is 6:40 p.m., the draft reads well, and
you know now what a sentence you did not write can cost. What, specifically,
do you do differently with the fourteenth note?

Date the file. Reread it at the end of intern year. Half of your class will
have moved, and the useful skill is noticing why.

## Summary

- No US malpractice claim involving a clinical AI tool has reached a verdict.
  What exists is a framework, a boundary, one experiment, and your position.
- The physician is measured against the standard of care; the AI is evidence,
  not a defendant. "The AI was wrong" is not a legal theory.
- The most exposed cell is following a tool into nonstandard care; the second
  is overriding a tool that was right. Jurors, in two studies, reward
  following the tool when it agrees with the standard.
- A biased model cut clinician accuracy by 11 points, and explanations did not
  significantly repair it.
- Four criteria draw the device line; the fourth, whether you can independently
  review the basis with time to do so, decides most cases. The guidance moved
  twice in January 2026.
- A PCCP is how a changing model stays cleared. Cleared is not validated.
- You sign it, you own it; the patient has to know; and there is a contract, or
  there is not.
- The tool can change you. Decide what you keep.
- Mr. Alvarez's sentence was written by nobody. Your name is on it.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The 2×2 [@pmid:31584609] and the *NEJM* liability analysis [@pmid:38231630],
  read together; then the two juror experiments [@pmid:32978285;
  @pmid:42242875].
- Jabbour in full, including the vignettes and the explanation format that
  did not help [@pmid:38112814].
- What scribes get wrong, measured: the academic-system pilot [@pmid:41996389]
  and a head-to-head of five platforms on simulated encounters, where 19.5% of
  transcript errors reached the note and an average of three errors per case
  had potential for moderate-to-severe harm [@pmid:41234546]. A scoping review
  in emergency medicine adds the equity finding: the speech-recognition layer
  under these tools has higher word error rates for Black speakers than White
  speakers, so the patient most likely to be misdocumented is not random
  [@pmid:42110031].
- Consent as it actually happens in clinic [@pmid:40694347].
- Deskilling [@pmid:40816301], and a 2026 systematic review of automation bias
  and deskilling with generative tools [@pmid:42445869].
- Cleared is not validated [@pmid:33820998; @pmid:39187696].
- The National Academy of Medicine's AI Code of Conduct, discussion draft
  [@pmid:39830818] and the informatics community's commentary on it
  [@pmid:39658328]; the 2025 final is a NAM publication and is scavenger-hunt
  question 7.
- Eight guiding principles for AI tools in health care
  [@doi:10.1038/s43856-023-00279-9], a useful checklist to test your Part B
  ruling against.

- [AI and machine learning for an oncology service line](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-28-ai-ml-oncology-service-line/):
  a campus governance framework and the eight guiding principles, which is what
  the committee you will one day sit on is trying to build.
